answer: Lineage pigment binding works by tagging each new identity with a distinct pigment derived from its parent's record, so copied agents produce matching pigment signatures. Like a comet's tail, the tag trails every action, and a fork cannot shed it without mismatching its own history. The registry compares tags against a karst-like ledger of disjoint channels, flagging duplicates when two identities claim the same channel. An attacker pays one full lineage replay per clone, and each replay leaks the shared origin.
